rv.q: This strategy does help the show steer clear of therapeutic bromides and conventional catharsis, but it creates a different problem: “Grief Camp,” which leans heavily on whimsy, feels unmoored, tentative.
Grief Camp offers a strikingly unsentimental and thoughtful panorama of young people who refuse to let grief hold them back from living.
Grief Camp offers plenty of room for humor and for touching insights into the ways we move about our lives carrying memories both burdensome and beautiful.
Grief Camp is a banquet of perfectly meshed design, fully inhabited by the lovable, convincing cast.
It’s a beautiful moment in an imperfect, strange play I won’t soon forget.

Theatergoers who prefer straightforward dramas with easily identifiable peaks and valleys are likely to be frustrated by Grief Camp, a play that meanders, digresses, and patently refuses to indulge the audience’s desire for tragedy porn.
The other, Grief Camp, by Eliya Smith (making her Off-Broadway debut), is decently directed at the Atlantic by Les Waters, but it’s dramatically flat and emotionally uninvolving.
Unfortunately, it proves sturdier than the play.
Unfortunately, that ends up turning Grief Camp into an Annie Baker-style writing exercise, where the playwright discovers that she’s not Annie Baker.
You'll want to fill yourself up with this deliciously complex meal before it goes away.
What you get instead is a string of moments—each a tiny pearl—that, taken together, form a quietly resonant necklace of meaning.
Grief Camp creates a vivid, fully inhabited world and assembles conditions ripe for drama, but never shapes them into a story.
Grief Camp, like the campers it depicts, is stuck in an inchoate space where it has not yet come to terms with all its issues.
This is one of the strongest shows of the off-Broadway season.

Smith and Tony-nominated director Les Waters (Dana H., Big Love) carefully avoid any lapses into sentimentality or solipsism, treating Cade and the campers like unique characters in their own right and not as plot points to rhapsodize about grief.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Smith's naturalistic debut: some praise its lived-in authenticity and humane portrayal of adolescent grief, while others find it aimless and unmoored, with whimsy overshadowing emotional depth.

vr.q: I think by the end, it has given you plenty to chew on and is very satisfying in that sense.
